learningObjectives.title: The alliance system and international crises (Morocco and the Balkans)
Anglo-German rivalry and the outbreak of war
The First World War: stalemate on the Western Front and the wider war

questions.q: Which three countries formed the Triple Alliance?
options: Britain, France and Russia
Germany, Austria-Hungary and Italy
Germany, Russia and Italy
France, Russia and Serbia
questions.explain: The Triple Alliance of 1882 bound Germany, Austria-Hungary and Italy together in mutual defence.

questions.q: Which powers made up the Triple Entente by 1907?
options: Britain, France and Russia
Germany, Austria-Hungary and Italy
Britain, Germany and France
France, Serbia and Belgium
questions.explain: The Triple Entente was an understanding between Britain, France and Russia, completed by the Anglo-Russian agreement of 1907.

questions.q: Why did the First Moroccan (Tangier) Crisis of 1905 increase tension in Europe?
options: Germany seized Morocco and made it a colony
France and Germany signed a formal alliance
Kaiser Wilhelm II's visit to Tangier challenged French control and drew Britain and France closer together
Britain abandoned its support for France
questions.explain: The Kaiser's intervention backfired, strengthening the Entente rather than dividing Britain and France.

questions.q: In which year did Austria-Hungary annex Bosnia, angering Serbia and Russia?
questions.explain: The 1908 annexation of Bosnia inflamed Slav nationalism and worsened relations between Austria-Hungary and Serbia.

questions.q: A historian argues the alliance system turned a local Balkan dispute into a European war. Which sequence of events best supports this claim?
options: Britain declared war on Serbia, prompting Germany to defend France
Italy invaded France, forcing Russia to attack Austria-Hungary
Serbia declared war on Germany, drawing in Britain and Italy
Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia, Russia mobilised to defend Serbia, and Germany then declared war on Russia and France
questions.explain: The chain of alliance obligations dragged the major powers into a wider conflict within days of the Austro-Serbian dispute.

questions.q: The Anglo-German naval race centred on the building of which powerful new type of battleship?
options: The U-boat
The ironclad
The Dreadnought
The man-of-war
questions.explain: Britain's launch of HMS Dreadnought in 1906 sparked an arms race as Germany tried to match the Royal Navy.

questions.q: What is meant by Britain's policy of 'splendid isolation' before the early 1900s?
options: Avoiding permanent alliances and staying out of European entanglements
Refusing to trade with other European countries
Building an empire only within Europe
Forming a formal military alliance with Germany
questions.explain: Britain traditionally avoided binding continental alliances, but growing German rivalry pushed it towards France and Russia.

questions.q: Whose assassination in Sarajevo on 28 June 1914 helped trigger the war?
options: Kaiser Wilhelm II of Germany
Archduke Franz Ferdinand of Austria-Hungary
Tsar Nicholas II of Russia
King George V of Britain
questions.explain: The heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne was shot in Sarajevo, sparking the July Crisis.

questions.q: Who assassinated Archduke Franz Ferdinand, and to which group did he belong?
options: Gavrilo Princip, a member of the Bolsheviks
Otto von Bismarck, a member of the Black Hand
Gavrilo Princip, a member of the Black Hand
Leon Trotsky, a member of the Serbian army
questions.explain: Princip was a Bosnian Serb linked to the nationalist Black Hand organisation.

questions.q: Why did Germany's invasion of Belgium in 1914 bring Britain into the war?
options: Britain had a formal military alliance with Germany
Belgium was a British colony
Britain had guaranteed Belgian neutrality under the 1839 Treaty of London
Britain wanted to seize Belgian territory
questions.explain: Britain used the violation of Belgian neutrality, guaranteed in 1839, as its reason for declaring war on Germany.

questions.q: What was the main aim of the Schlieffen Plan?
options: To defeat France quickly through Belgium before turning to fight Russia, avoiding a war on two fronts
To defeat Russia first and then invade Britain
To defend Germany's borders without attacking
To capture Britain's navy in the North Sea
questions.explain: Germany hoped for a swift knock-out of France in the west before Russia could fully mobilise in the east.

questions.q: Why was the Battle of the Marne (September 1914) significant?
options: It resulted in Germany capturing Paris
It halted the German advance on Paris and led to the trench warfare and stalemate on the Western Front
It forced Russia out of the war
It was the first naval battle of the war
questions.explain: The Marne stopped the Schlieffen Plan's advance and both sides then dug in, beginning years of stalemate.

questions.q: In which year did the Battle of the Somme take place?
questions.explain: The Somme offensive was fought from July to November 1916, becoming a symbol of costly attrition.

questions.q: What was Germany's main strategy at the Battle of Verdun in 1916?
options: To 'bleed France white' by inflicting massive casualties in a war of attrition
To break through and capture Paris in a single day
To surround and destroy the British navy
To force Russia to surrender
questions.explain: Falkenhayn aimed to inflict unsustainable losses on France at the fortress city of Verdun.

questions.q: A soldier's 1916 diary describes advancing slowly across muddy no man's land into machine-gun fire and barbed wire, with enormous British casualties on the first day. Which battle is he most likely describing?
options: The Battle of the Marne
The Battle of the Somme
The Battle of Jutland
The Gallipoli landings
questions.explain: The first day of the Somme (1 July 1916) saw around 57,000 British casualties advancing against machine guns and wire.

questions.q: What was the name of the major 1916 naval battle between the British Grand Fleet and the German High Seas Fleet?
options: The Battle of the Somme
The Battle of Trafalgar
The Battle of Jutland
The Battle of Tsushima
questions.explain: Jutland (1916) was the war's largest naval battle; though tactically inconclusive, it left Britain in control of the seas.

questions.q: In 1917 German unrestricted submarine warfare was sinking huge numbers of Allied merchant ships. Which Allied response most effectively reduced these losses?
options: Grouping merchant ships together under naval escort in the convoy system
Withdrawing all ships from the Atlantic
Building larger, slower cargo ships
Abandoning the blockade of Germany
questions.explain: The convoy system, introduced in 1917, sharply cut shipping losses by protecting merchant vessels with warship escorts.

questions.q: What was the main consequence of the USA entering the war in 1917?
options: It forced Britain to leave the war
It provided the Allies with fresh troops, supplies and money, tipping the balance against Germany
It had no real impact on the fighting
It caused Russia to rejoin the war
questions.explain: American manpower and resources gave the Allies a decisive long-term advantage over an exhausted Germany.

questions.q: What was the significance of the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk in 1918?
options: It brought the USA into the war
It ended the war between Britain and Germany
Russia withdrew from the war, allowing Germany to move troops to the Western Front
It created the League of Nations
questions.explain: Russia's exit freed German divisions from the east, enabling the 1918 Spring Offensive in the west.

questions.q: Germany launched its major 'Spring Offensive' (Ludendorff Offensive) in early 1918. Why was this timing chosen?
options: To try to win the war before large numbers of American troops arrived on the Western Front
Because the German navy had just defeated Britain
Because Russia had just entered the war on Germany's side
Because the trenches had finally been abandoned
questions.explain: Germany gambled on a knock-out blow in spring 1918 before the growing American army could tip the balance.

specSource: AQA GCSE History (8145) specification; Conflict and Tension, 1894-1918 (First World War)
